{{Short description|Fourier series type expansion}}
'''Schlömilch's series''' is a [[Fourier series]] type expansion of twice continuously differentiable function in the interval <math>(0,\pi)</math> in terms of the [[Bessel function of the first kind]], named after the German mathematician [[Oskar Schlömilch]], who derived the series in 1857.<ref>Schlomilch, G. (1857). On Bessel's function. Zeitschrift fur Math, and Phys., 2, 155-158.</ref><ref>[[E. T. Whittaker|Whittaker, E. T.]], & [[G. N. Watson|Watson, G. N.]] (1996). [[A Course of Modern Analysis]]. Cambridge university press.</ref><ref>[[John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh|Lord Rayleigh]] (1911). LXII. On a physical interpretation of Schlömilch's theorem in Bessel's functions. The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science, 21(124), 567-571.</ref><ref>[[G. N. Watson|Watson, G. N.]] (1995). A treatise on the theory of Bessel functions. Cambridge university press.</ref><ref>Chapman, S. (1911). On the general theory of summability, with application to Fourier's and other series. Quarterly Journal, 43, 1-52.</ref> The real-valued function <math>f(x)</math> has the following expansion:

:<math>f(x) = a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n J_0(nx),</math>

where

:<math>\begin{align}
a_0 &= f(0) + \frac{1}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \int_0^{\pi/2} u f'(u\sin\theta)\ d\theta\ du, \\
a_n &= \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \int_0^{\pi/2} u\cos nu \ f'(u\sin\theta)\ d\theta\ du.
\end{align}</math>

==Examples==
Some examples of Schlömilch's series are the following:
*Null functions in the interval <math>(0,\pi)</math> can be expressed by Schlömilch's Series, <math>0 = \frac{1}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n J_0(nx)</math>, which cannot be obtained by [[Fourier Series]]. This is particularly interesting because the null function is represented by a series expansion in which not all the coefficients are zero. The series converges only when <math>0<x<\pi</math>; the series oscillates at <math>x=0</math> and diverges at <math>x=\pi</math>. This theorem is generalized so that <math>0 = \frac{1}{2\Gamma(\nu+1)}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n J_0(nx)/(nx/2)^\nu</math> when <math>-1/2<\nu\leq 1/2</math> and <math>0<x<\pi</math> and also when <math>\nu> 1/2</math> and <math>0<x\leq \pi</math>. These properties were identified by [[Niels Nielsen (mathematician)|Niels Nielsen]].<ref>Nielsen, N. (1904). Handbuch der theorie der cylinderfunktionen. BG Teubner.</ref>
*<math>x = \frac{\pi^2}{4}-2\sum_{n=1,3,...}^\infty \frac{J_0(nx)}{n^2}, \quad 0<x<\pi.</math>
*<math>x^2 = \frac{2\pi^2}{3} + 8 \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}J_0(nx), \quad -\pi<x<\pi.</math>
*<math>\frac{1}{x} + \sum_{m=1}^k\frac{2}{\sqrt{x^2-4m^2\pi^2}} = \frac{1}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty J_0(nx), \quad 2k\pi<x<2(k+1)\pi.</math>
* If <math>(r,z)</math> are the cylindrical polar coordinates, then the series <math>1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty e^{-nz}J_0(nr)</math> is a solution of [[Laplace equation]] for <math>z>0</math>.
